lead: A rectifier is judged from both sides. On the DC side the question is how much ripple rides on the average; on the AC side it is how much of the input current is useful in-phase fundamental, which sets the power factor and the harmonic pollution. This chapter defines the standard performance parameters, works them out for the usual converters, and lists the ways the power factor of a phase-controlled converter is improved.
prereq: You need: the output waveforms and supply currents of single-phase and three-phase controlled rectifiers, and Fourier series of a square wave.

sections.h3: Output side: form factor, ripple factor and TUF

blocks.text: Take an output voltage vo(t) of period T. Its average Vdc carries the useful DC power; its RMS Vrms sets the heating. The ripple is what is left after the average is removed, and the RMS values add in quadrature: Vrms² = Vdc² + Vac², where Vac is the RMS of the ripple.
FF = Vrms/Vdc;   RF = Vac/Vdc = √(FF² − 1);   CF = Vpeak/Vrms;   TUF = Pdc/(Vs Is)
blocks.where: FF is the form factor, RF the ripple factor, CF the crest factor with Vpeak the highest instantaneous value, and TUF the transformer utilisation factor with Vs, Is the RMS voltage and current of the transformer secondary. The rectification efficiency Pdc/Pac = (Vdc/Vrms)² for a resistive load.

blocks.text: Typical values with a resistive load and no firing delay: half-wave RF = 1.21, single-phase bridge RF = 0.482, three-phase bridge RF = 0.042. The ripple frequency is p f, where p is the pulse number.

sections.h3: Input side: displacement, distortion and power factor

blocks.text: The supply voltage is close to a sine, but the input current is not. Write its total RMS as Is and the RMS of its fundamental as I1. Only the fundamental carries average power with a sinusoidal voltage, so
PF = P/S = (Vs I1 cos φ1)/(Vs Is) = (I1/Is) × cos φ1 = g × DF
blocks.where: φ1 is the angle by which the fundamental current lags the voltage; DF = cos φ1 is the displacement factor; g = I1/Is is the distortion factor (some books call it the current distortion factor, a few use DF for it, so read the definition).
HF is the harmonic factor, the RMS of all the harmonics divided by the fundamental; most syllabi call it the total harmonic distortion.

blocks.text: Single-phase fully controlled bridge, continuous current. The supply current is a square wave of height Id, shifted by α. Its fundamental peak is 4Id/π, so I1 = (2√2/π) Id = 0.900 Id while Is = Id. Hence g = 0.900, THD = 48.3 % and DF = cos α, giving PF = 0.900 cos α. The harmonics are odd only, with In = I1/n: the 3rd is 33 %, the 5th 20 %, the 7th 14 %.

Three-phase bridge. Each line carries 120° blocks of ±Id: Is = 0.816 Id, I1 = 0.780 Id, so g = 3/π = 0.955, THD = 31.1 %, DF = cos α and PF = 0.955 cos α. A p-pulse converter has only the characteristic harmonics h = kp ± 1 (k = 1, 2, 3 …): 5, 7, 11, 13 … for p = 6. The DC output ripple sits at multiples of p f.
The displacement factor cos α falls as the output is turned down, and the converter draws reactive power Q1 = Vs I1 sin α even when it delivers little DC power. The usual remedies are:

items: Freewheeling diode or half-controlled bridge: the supply current flows only from α to π, so DF = cos(α/2) instead of cos α.
Extinction angle control: self-commutated switches turn on at the zero crossing and off before π, so the fundamental leads.
Symmetrical angle control: the switches conduct for a window centred on the voltage peak, so φ1 = 0 and DF = 1 at every output.
PWM control: many sine-weighted pulses per half-cycle push the harmonics up to frequencies a small filter removes.
Sequence control: two series bridges, one held at full output while the other is phase controlled, so only half of the voltage is ever delayed.
Shunt capacitors and harmonic filters on the AC side, or a PFC rectifier.

examples.question: A single-phase fully controlled bridge on 230 V, 50 Hz carries a level load current Id = 10 A at α = 30°. Find I1, g, THD, DF, PF, the real and reactive input power, and check the power against the DC side.
steps: DC side: Vdc = 207.07 × 0.866 = 179.33 V, so Vdc Id = 1793 W, equal to P, as it must be for an ideal converter.

examples.question: The three-phase bridge of the earlier example (400 V, α = 30°, Vdc = 467.82 V) carries Id = 50 A. Find the line RMS current, I1, PF, THD and the 5th and 7th harmonic currents.
steps: I5 = I1/5 = 7.80 A and I7 = I1/7 = 5.57 A; there is no 3rd harmonic.

traps: Writing PF = cos α. That is only the displacement factor; the distortion factor (0.900 or 0.955) multiplies it.
Listing even harmonics or a 3rd harmonic for a three-phase bridge. Half-wave symmetry removes the even ones, and the 120° blocks remove the triplens: only 6k ± 1 remain.
Computing RF from Vpeak − Vdc. RF uses the RMS of the ripple: √(FF² − 1).
Subtracting THD from 1 to get g. They are linked by g = 1/√(1 + THD²).
Mixing up DF: in some books it is the displacement factor, in others the distortion factor. State the definition you use.

quiz.q: Define ripple factor and give it in terms of the form factor.
quiz.a: RF = RMS of the AC ripple / average = √(FF² − 1), with FF = Vrms/Vdc.

quiz.q: Define displacement factor, distortion factor and harmonic factor.
quiz.a: Displacement factor = cos φ1, the cosine of the angle between the fundamental current and the voltage. Distortion factor g = I1/Is. Harmonic factor = THD = √(Is² − I1²)/I1.

quiz.q: Why is a converter's power factor written as g × cos φ1?
quiz.a: With a sinusoidal voltage only the fundamental current gives average power, P = Vs I1 cos φ1, while S = Vs Is. So PF = P/S = (I1/Is) cos φ1: one factor for the waveform shape and one for the phase shift.

quiz.q: A single-phase fully controlled bridge with level current Id = 20 A runs at α = 60°. Find I1, PF and THD.
A rectifier has PF = 0.70 and displacement factor 0.90. Find the distortion factor and THD.
At α = 60° with Id = 10 A, compare the PF of a fully controlled and a half-controlled single-phase bridge.
quiz.a: Full: square wave, g = 0.900, DF = cos 60° = 0.5, PF = 0.450. Half-controlled: current blocks 120° wide, Is = 10√(120/180) = 8.16 A, I1 = 0.9003 × 10 × cos 30° = 7.80 A, g = 0.955, DF = cos 30° = 0.866, PF = 0.827. The half-controlled bridge draws much less reactive power at the same α.

quiz.q: At α = 90° the current of a fully controlled bridge is still a full square wave. Why is the power factor zero?
quiz.a: The fundamental lags the voltage by 90°, so cos φ1 = 0 and P = Vs I1 cos φ1 = 0, although g is still 0.900. The converter draws only reactive power and harmonics.

beyond: Not for the exam. IEC 61000-3-2 limits the harmonic currents of equipment up to 16 A per phase and IEEE 519 those of a whole plant. Utilities also bill reactive power, so large thyristor drives come with capacitor banks and tuned filters. Search for 'total demand distortion' and 'tuned harmonic filter'.
